::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## **IN PROGRESS:** Ocean Power Technologies (OPTT): Machine Learning and Risk Modeling

In this project, I analyse the stock ticker OPTT (Ocean Power Technologies). It is a stock that has 
long suffered after immediate and rapid success, now residing as a penny stock trading for less than $0.50.

Recently, they signed a $6.5 million deal with the US government, giving the company a chance to pivot their
business model into something (potentially) profitable. 

In this analysis, I use an OLS Regression to analyse the stock's historical performance and an ordinal logistic regression dive into the probability of specific risk levels. I then use a factor model to analyse the drivers of the company's underlying risk. 

Moreover, I use Ridge Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and LSTM Network algorithms to predict 
future performance. My main goal is to better understand how to analyse stocks using statistical modelling, while 
also looking into the limitations of single-algorithm machine learning techniques when predicting stock performance. 

My end-goal is not to have a perfect predictive model (although that would be nice). Rather, I intend to keep at this project for an extended period of time to deepen my understanding of the core mathematical concepts as well as my understanding of each model - the benefits, the limitations, efficiency, etc.  

This project is currently still underway, but feel free to check out my progress on my github repo!
Once finished, I will also upload a rendered PDF output of my full report with visualisations and analysis. 

**Want to dive into my work? My progress is live on GitHub:**

[View Progress](https://github.com/ojreece/Machine-Learning-Predictive-Modelling){.btn .btn-outline-primary}

:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## **IN PROGESS:** Risk Factor Modelling with Principal Component Analysis

In this project, my goal is simple: construct a basic factor model to determine risk for the S&P500. 

I use principal component analysis because it allows me to compress many correlated variables into a collection of perfectly uncorrelated drivers of risk.

I also use CAPM, 3-factor and 5-factor models to act as a point of comparison, with a final comparison model incorporating risk free assets (bonds). 

I begin this project in R, and as I develop my python skills further I plan to recreate the project in python. My reasoning is that python will be more useful to understand in a professional finance setting. 

Furthermore, while doing this project in R, I am not simply using the functions built in that would help speed up the creation of the PCA, even though that would be more efficient. Instead I am doing the majority of the math step by step such that I gain a better understanding of the underlying theory. WHen I transition to python, I will skip this and just use the simpler steps, using the built in functions. 

Credit for the inspiration behind this project:

- Professor Robert Kissell (Using PCA for Factor Model)
- Professor Nusret Cakici (Factor Model Foundation, Arguments against using PCA)
- Professor Michael Cheah (Addition of bonds)


[View Progress](https://github.com/ojreece/Factor_Model_PCA){.btn .btn-outline-primary}
:::
